content: Croup is a common respiratory illness in children, characterized by a distinctive barking cough, stridor (a high-pitched wheezing sound during breathing), hoarseness, and respiratory distress. In severe cases, children with croup may require intubation to secure their airway. Nebulized epinephrine has been proposed as a treatment to reduce the need for intubation in these cases. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of nebulized epinephrine compared to placebo in children with croup. Effectiveness was assessed using croup scores, rates of intubation, and healthcare utilization metrics such as hospitalization rates. Safety was evaluated by examining the frequency and severity of side effects. The study also compared racemic epinephrine to L-epinephrine (a specific isomer) and assessed the impact of delivering nebulized epinephrine with intermittent positive pressure breathing (IPPB) versus standard nebulization. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Web of Science, CINAHL, and Scopus, covering studies published up to mid-2013. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs involving children with croup who were evaluated in emergency departments or hospitalized. The primary outcome was the change in croup scores after treatment, while secondary outcomes included intubation rates, hospitalization duration, return visits for croup, parental anxiety, and side effects. Eight studies involving a total of 225 participants were included in the analysis. Most of the children in these studies were under two years of age, and their croup severity was described as moderate to severe. Six studies were conducted in inpatient settings, one in an emergency department, and one in an unspecified setting. Six of the eight studies were judged to have a low risk of bias, while the remaining two had an unclear risk of bias. Nebulized epinephrine was found to significantly improve croup scores 30 minutes after treatment (based on three RCTs, standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.94; 95% confidence interval [CI] -1.37 to -0.51). However, this improvement was not sustained at two and six hours post-treatment. Additionally, nebulized epinephrine was associated with a significantly shorter hospital stay compared to placebo in one study (mean difference [MD] -32.0 hours; 95% CI -59.1 to -4.9). When comparing racemic epinephrine to L-epinephrine, no significant difference in croup scores was observed 30 minutes after treatment (SMD 0.33; 95% CI -0.42 to 1.08). However, after two hours, L-epinephrine demonstrated a significant reduction in croup scores compared to racemic epinephrine in one study (SMD 0.87; 95% CI 0.09 to 1.65). There was no significant difference in croup scores between nebulized epinephrine delivered via IPPB and standard nebulization at 30 minutes (SMD -0.14; 95% CI -1.24 to 0.95) or two hours (SMD -0.72; 95% CI -1.86 to 0.42). None of the included studies reported data on adverse effects of nebulized epinephrine. In conclusion, nebulized epinephrine provides a clinically and statistically significant, but transient, reduction in croup symptoms 30 minutes after treatment. There is no clear evidence favoring racemic epinephrine over L-epinephrine or the use of IPPB over standard nebulization. However, the findings are limited by the small number of studies and participants, with many outcomes relying on data from very few or even single studies.
